title: Information Cascades in the Laboratory
description: Six decision makers sequentially predict which urn generated private light or dark draws. Later decision makers observe earlier public predictions but not earlier private draws. Treatments alter whether two public draws appear after the fourth prediction and whether the two urns have symmetric or asymmetric compositions.

included: participant-facing procedure reconstructed from the published Appendix
public unpaid practice until urn A and urn B have each appeared
two symmetric sessions with two public draws after the fourth prediction
six asymmetric sessions with urn A containing 6 light and 1 dark ball and urn B containing 5 light and 2 dark balls
equal prior probability of urn A and urn B
new random decision order in every paid period
excluded: the third symmetric public-draw session, because its draw timing and treatment procedure are not specified
a seventh human monitor as an agent role
physical partitions, marbles, envelopes, room logistics, and cash handling
replay of unavailable participant-level raw decisions
implementation_scope.reason: All treatments whose participant information and timing can be recovered from the article are implemented as generative environments. Raw outcome data are not required to recreate randomized urn selections and draws. The one public-draw session whose procedure is not described remains excluded so the package does not invent participant-facing information.

findings.main_hypothesis: When prior public information dominates a conflicting private signal, later participants often follow an information cascade.
Sequential public predictions improve information-use efficiency relative to decisions based only on private signals.
With asymmetric signal informativeness, simple counting explains a substantial subset of deviations from Bayesian choice.
